title: Maximum Alternating Subarray Sum With One Deletion
descriptionHtml:
You are given an integer array nums.

You may delete at most one element from nums, then choose a subarray of the resulting array.

Return the maximum possible alternating sum of the chosen subarray.

The alternating sum of an array is the sum of its elements at even indices minus the sum of its elements at odd indices. The chosen subarray is reindexed starting from 0 before calculating its alternating sum.

 

Example 1:

Input: nums = [5,-5,1]

Output: 11

Explanation:

Choose not to delete an element and select the entire array. Its alternating sum is 5 - (-5) + 1 = 11, which is the maximum possible.

Example 2:

Input: nums = [10,-5,-100]

Output: 110

Explanation:

Delete nums[1] = -5 to obtain [10,-100], then select the entire resulting array. Its alternating sum is 10 - (-100) = 110, which is the maximum possible.

Example 3:

Input: nums = [4,7]

Output: 7

Explanation:

Choose not to delete an element and select the subarray [7]. Its alternating sum is 7, which is the maximum possible.

 

Constraints:

  • 1 <= nums.length <= 105
  • -105 <= nums[i] <= 105
explanationMarkdown:
### Track retained-length parity and whether deletion has been used

Every chosen subarray starts with a plus sign. Appending a retained element alternates the sign; deleting an element does not change the parity of the retained length. These are exactly the two properties needed for a constant-size dynamic program.

Use four states `dp[used][parity]`. `used` is zero or one according to whether the deletion has been used. In the implementation, parity zero means an odd number of retained elements, so the last retained element was added; parity one means an even number, so the last retained element was subtracted. Each state represents a nonempty candidate reaching the current processed position, which may itself have been deleted.

For the next value `x`, calculate every transition from the previous states:

- Without deletion, an odd-length candidate is either a new singleton `[x]` or an even-length candidate extended by `+x`: `new[0][0] = max(old[0][1], 0) + x`.
- An even-length candidate without deletion must extend an odd-length candidate: `new[0][1] = old[0][0] - x`.
- With deletion used, an odd-length candidate either extends a previously deleted even-length candidate by `+x`, or deletes `x` from a no-deletion odd-length candidate: `new[1][0] = max(old[1][1] + x, old[0][0])`.
- Similarly, `new[1][1] = max(old[1][0] - x, old[0][1])`.

The code updates the deletion row first so its transitions still read the old no-deletion row. Each row assignment evaluates its entire right-hand side before replacing that row. Initialize all states and the answer to negative infinity, and take the best state after every position.

### Why this finds the optimum

At a position inside the candidate, the only legal choices are keeping that element or using the single deletion on it. Keeping toggles retained-length parity; deleting preserves it. The four transitions enumerate both choices and every possible starting position. Taking the maximum across positions allows the chosen subarray to end anywhere. Deleting an element outside the chosen subarray adds no useful option, since the same subarray is already considered with no deletion.

### Edge cases

The answer must be nonempty, even when every value is negative. In particular, a singleton negative input returns that negative value, not zero. A deletion can change the signs of every following retained element, so treating it as merely subtracting the removed value is incorrect. Use 64-bit integers in C++ because the answer can exceed a 32-bit signed integer; guard negative-infinity states before arithmetic.

### Complexity

**Time:** O(n), where n is nums.length; each element updates four states.

**Space:** O(1) auxiliary space.
